ripple_effect.name: Persian Gulf oil supply shock

historical_precedents.what_happened: Iran and Iraq attacked oil tankers transiting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and Iran repeatedly threatened to close the strait.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Shipping insurance war-risk premiums in the Gulf rose sharply, and the U.S. Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 to keep the strait open.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large share of Gulf oil exports from the market and raised fears of a wider regional war.

Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.

ripple_effect.name: Major cryptocurrency regulatory shift or exchange collapse

historical_precedents.what_happened: Chinese regulators intensified action against cryptocurrency mining and trading through 2021, and in September 2021 the government declared all cryptocurrency transactions illegal.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Bitcoin's price fell to around $30,000 following the initial May 2021 wave of regulatory action, and China-based mining operations relocated to other countries as the crackdown intensified.

historical_precedents.event: El Salvador adopts, then walks back, Bitcoin as legal tender
historical_precedents.what_happened: El Salvador's Legislative Assembly approved making Bitcoin legal tender on June 9, 2021, taking effect September 7, 2021; the IMF warned in January 2022 that the move posed risks to financial stability and consumer protection and linked concerns about the policy to a proposed $1.3 billion loan.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Bitcoin's price fell roughly 45% between September 2021 and January 2022, and El Salvador's reserves lost an estimated $22 million from the currency's depreciation over that period; as part of a $1.4 billion IMF loan agreement reached in December 2024, El Salvador agreed to end mandatory merchant acceptance of Bitcoin, formalized in a February 2025 legal amendment.

historical_precedents.event: Collapse of the FTX cryptocurrency exchange
historical_precedents.what_happened: FTX's solvency crisis unfolded over days in early November 2022, from reports of concentrated exposure to its FTT token through a failed rescue bid by rival exchange Binance, before FTX filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on November 11, 2022, with CEO Sam Bankman-Fried resigning.
historical_precedents.market_impact: FTX was found to owe as much as $8 billion, prompting SEC and CFTC investigations and federal charges against Bankman-Fried in December 2022; a bankruptcy court later ordered FTX's estate to pay $12.7 billion in compensation to former customers in August 2024.

possibility_chains: A major national ban or crackdown on cryptocurrency activity has historically caused an immediate drop in crypto prices, followed by a longer-run relocation of affected activity (such as mining) to jurisdictions with friendlier rules.

A high-profile exchange collapse has historically prompted regulators worldwide to accelerate consumer-protection and market-structure rulemaking for the crypto industry, even in jurisdictions not directly affected.

Sovereign adoption of a cryptocurrency as legal tender has historically drawn scrutiny from multilateral lenders like the IMF over financial-stability risk, given the currency's price volatility relative to a country's fiscal and reserve needs.

A major national ban or crackdown on cryptocurrency activity has historically caused an immediate drop in crypto prices, followed by a longer-run relocation of affected activity (such as mining) to jurisdictions with friendlier rules.

ripple_effect.name: African swine fever outbreak collapses China's pork supply

historical_precedents.event: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd
historical_precedents.what_happened: China's first confirmed case of African swine fever was reported in Liaoning province in August 2018 (with more than 38,000 hogs culled within the first two weeks); within about eight months the disease had spread to every region of China. China's pig population fell by almost 100 million head compared with the previous year — roughly a quarter of the global pig population affected. The disease also spread through Southeast Asia, reaching Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production.

possibility_chains: A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

Countries hit by a major livestock epidemic have historically accelerated biosecurity investment and herd-rebuilding programs, a process that has typically taken multiple years to restore pre-outbreak production levels.

A large, sudden loss of one protein source has historically shifted consumer demand toward substitute proteins (e.g. poultry, beef, or soy-based products) in the affected country, with knock-on price effects in those markets.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd (August 2018 – 2019): The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production. A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

linked_playbooks.name: Avian influenza outbreak drives poultry and egg price shock
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) forces mass culling of U.S. egg-laying hens (2022 onward): The mass culling sharply reduced the U.S. egg-laying flock and was followed by 'skyrocketing' egg prices, a pattern that recurred with further culling waves in subsequent years; egg producers such as Cal-Maine later faced scrutiny, including litigation over pricing coordination between 2022 and 2025, during the shortage period. A major livestock disease outbreak that forces large-scale culling has historically produced protein-specific price spikes (e.g. eggs or poultry) within months, distinct from broader crop-driven food inflation.

linked_playbooks.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Four underwater explosions in the Baltic Sea near Bornholm Island ruptured three of the four Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipeline strings, which ran directly from Russia to Germany. Countries heavily dependent on a single pipeline supplier have historically faced the sharpest price spikes and, in the most severe cases, direct supply shortfalls during a cutoff.
Sustained higher natural gas costs have historically raised electricity prices in gas-reliant power grids and increased costs for gas-intensive industries such as fertilizer and chemicals production.

linked_playbooks.name: G7 price cap on sanctioned oil exports
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: G7/EU/Australia price cap on Russian seaborne crude oil (December 2022 onward): Russian crude traded well below the cap in the following weeks — reported as low as about $45 a barrel at Baltic ports — and Russia's weekly oil export duty revenue reportedly fell by around 60%; Russia responded by building a large 'shadow fleet' of older tankers (estimated at over 1,000 vessels by late 2023) operating outside Western insurance and shipping services to sell oil above the cap. ripple_effect.name: Medical tourism as a cross-border healthcare cost arbitrage

historical_precedents.event: Growth of outbound US medical tourism and inbound medical-tourism hub economies
historical_precedents.what_happened: An estimated 750,000 Americans traveled abroad for medical care in 2007, with Deloitte projecting the flow could grow roughly tenfold over the following decade; by 2015 estimates of US outbound medical tourists seeking inpatient care ranged from 150,000 to 320,000 annually, while destination countries built dedicated medical-tourism industries — Thailand drew an estimated 2.81 million foreign patients in 2015 (up 10.2% year-on-year) generating about $4.7 billion in 2013 revenue, and Jordan attracted about 250,000 international patients and companions in 2012, generating over $1 billion.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Lower-cost destination countries built hospital accreditation and marketing infrastructure specifically to capture price-sensitive patients from higher-cost systems like the US; India's medical tourism sector was projected (as of 2015) to grow about 30% annually from a 2012 base, potentially reaching $2 billion by 2015 — establishing medical tourism as a recurring, price-driven cross-border patient flow rather than a niche phenomenon.

possibility_chains: A large price gap between a patient's home healthcare system and a lower-cost destination with comparable hospital accreditation has historically been sufficient on its own to sustain outbound medical tourism flows, independent of any single trigger event.
Destination countries have historically used medical tourism revenue and hospital investment as a deliberate export-diversification strategy, as seen in Thailand, Jordan, and Vietnam.
A rise in domestic healthcare costs or insurance-coverage gaps in a patient's home country has historically correlated with an increase in outbound medical tourism from that country.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Growth of outbound US medical tourism and inbound medical-tourism hub economies (2007–2015): Lower-cost destination countries built hospital accreditation and marketing infrastructure specifically to capture price-sensitive patients from higher-cost systems like the US; India's medical tourism sector was projected (as of 2015) to grow about 30% annually from a 2012 base, potentially reaching $2 billion by 2015 — establishing medical tourism as a recurring, price-driven cross-border patient flow rather than a niche phenomenon. A large price gap between a patient's home healthcare system and a lower-cost destination with comparable hospital accreditation has historically been sufficient on its own to sustain outbound medical tourism flows, independent of any single trigger event.

linked_playbooks.name: Pharmaceutical patent cliff and blockbuster drug revenue loss
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Lipitor (atorvastatin) patent expiration (1996–2012 (US patent expired November 30, 2011)): Generic prices stayed relatively elevated during that initial exclusivity window, then fell sharply once additional manufacturers entered in May 2012, pushing a month's supply down toward standard generic pricing of $10 or less — illustrating the two-stage price collapse (moderate initial generic discount, then a much steeper one once multiple generic makers compete) that characterizes a typical pharmaceutical patent-cliff event. A cluster of blockbuster drugs (defined in the industry as over $1 billion in annual sales) losing patent protection in the same multi-year window has historically pushed large pharmaceutical companies toward M&A, portfolio diversification, and 'evergreening' strategies (new formulations or delivery mechanisms) to offset the revenue drop.

linked_playbooks.name: Health insurer exits from public exchanges and market instability
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: UnitedHealth Group's large-scale ACA exchange exit (April 2016 (effective 2017 plan year)): The exit — following the shortfall of the ACA's risk-corridors program, which lost up to $8.3 billion for the 2014–2015 plan years combined and triggered separate insurer litigation against the federal government — reduced plan choice and competition in many exchange markets for the 2017 plan year and became a recurring talking point in the 2016 US election-year debate over the ACA's stability. A change in the assumed risk pool or a shortfall in a program's risk-mitigation funding, as with the ACA's risk corridors, has historically led large insurers to reassess or exit a newly created insurance market before it stabilizes.

ripple_effect.name: Central bank interest rate hikes

historical_precedents.event: U.S. Federal Reserve's fastest rate-hiking cycle in decades
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate from near zero to over 5% in about 16 months, responding to the highest inflation in roughly 40 years.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The average 30-year U.S. mortgage rate roughly doubled from around 3% to over 7%, home sales slowed sharply, and high-growth technology stocks — more sensitive to rate changes — fell substantially more than the broader market in 2022.

historical_precedents.event: Fed Chair Paul Volcker's rate hikes to break double-digit inflation
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Fed raised interest rates to nearly 20% to bring runaway inflation under control.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The policy triggered a deep recession and a sharp rise in unemployment before inflation was brought down over the following years.

historical_precedents.event: European Central Bank rate hikes under Jean-Claude Trichet
historical_precedents.what_happened: The ECB raised its benchmark rate twice in 2011 (to 1.25% in April, then 1.5% in July) to fight headline inflation, even as the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis was worsening — Portugal's debt was downgraded to junk the same day as the July hike.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Peripheral Eurozone bond yields (Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece) surged in the following months as the debt crisis deepened; the hikes are widely regarded in hindsight as a policy mistake, and the ECB reversed course with cuts in November and December 2011 after Mario Draghi succeeded Trichet as president — a case where a rate-hike decision, unlike the Fed episodes above, is broadly seen as having worsened rather than merely responded to a crisis.

possibility_chains: Higher central bank interest rates have historically raised borrowing costs across the economy — mortgages, auto loans, and business credit — with mortgage and housing markets typically among the most sensitive.

Rate hikes have historically pressured stock valuations, particularly for growth-oriented companies whose profits are expected further in the future, since higher rates reduce the present value of those future earnings.
Aggressive rate-hiking cycles have historically raised the risk of an economic slowdown or recession, though the size and timing of that effect has varied a great deal across different hiking cycles.

Higher central bank interest rates have historically raised borrowing costs across the economy — mortgages, auto loans, and business credit — with mortgage and housing markets typically among the most sensitive.

ripple_effect.name: Minimum wage policy shift

historical_precedents.what_happened: The movement began in November 2012 when over 100 fast-food workers walked off the job in New York City demanding a $15 hourly wage and the right to unionize, at a time when the federal minimum wage had been frozen at $7.25 since 2009; it grew into coordinated multi-city strikes, including an April 2015 day of action across more than 200 cities that organizers called the largest protest by low-wage workers in US history.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By the mid-2020s seventeen US states plus Washington, D.C. had adopted $15-or-higher minimum wages, with organizers estimating roughly 26 million workers received a combined $151 billion in raises traceable to the movement's pressure on state and local policy.

historical_precedents.event: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage
historical_precedents.what_happened: Seattle's city council, led by councilmember Kshama Sawant, passed an ordinance phasing in a $15 minimum wage starting in 2014, with the wage rising further to $15.45 in 2018 and $16 in 2019 under the city's indexing formula.
historical_precedents.market_impact: University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate.

possibility_chains: A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

Employers in low-margin, labor-intensive sectors (fast food, retail, hospitality) have historically responded to minimum wage increases through some combination of price increases, reduced hours, and accelerated investment in self-service or automation technology, with the mix varying by study and locality.
Higher minimum wages have historically raised the wage floor workers use as a reference point in unrelated wage negotiations nearby, a "lighthouse effect" observed in several minimum-wage studies.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage (2014–2019): University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate. A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: California's Proposition 22 and its multi-year court challenge (November 2020 – July 2024): The nearly four-year legal uncertainty over Proposition 22's validity was itself a business risk for Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, and Instacart, which had spent over $200 million campaigning for the measure; its eventual affirmation cemented independent-contractor status for California gig drivers and became a template gig companies pushed for in other US states. A court or ballot-measure ruling on gig-worker classification in one jurisdiction has historically become a reference point cited by both labor advocates and gig companies lobbying for similar outcomes elsewhere, spreading the policy debate beyond the original jurisdiction.

linked_playbooks.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: The "Great Resignation" in the United States (March 2021 – mid-2023): Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023. A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Finance ministers from France, West Germany, Japan, the UK, and the US agreed at New York's Plaza Hotel to jointly intervene in currency markets to depreciate the US dollar, which had strengthened roughly 50% against major currencies between 1980 and 1985.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The dollar fell about 4% against other major currencies the Monday after the agreement was made public, and continued weakening over the following two years — a decline substantial enough that the G5/G7 later signed the 1987 Louvre Accord to halt it.

historical_precedents.event: US Dollar Index reaches a multi-decade high
historical_precedents.what_happened: A combination of aggressive Fed rate hikes, the war in Ukraine, and a resulting European energy crisis drove the US Dollar Index sharply higher through 2022.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The index closed 2022 at 110.05, its highest level since the early 1980s (it had peaked around 151.47 in 1984), squeezing countries and companies with dollar-denominated debt and import bills.

possibility_chains: A sharply stronger dollar has historically made dollar-denominated debt more expensive to service for foreign governments and companies that earn revenue in other currencies, raising default risk in the most exposed economies.
A strong dollar has historically weighed on the earnings of large US multinational companies, since revenue earned abroad translates back into fewer dollars.

Coordinated multi-country currency interventions, as in the Plaza Accord, have historically shown that large, sustained dollar moves can be at least partly reversed by deliberate policy action when major economies agree to act together — though such coordination has been rare.

ripple_effect.name: Major earthquake devastates a national economy and drives reconstruction financing

historical_precedents.what_happened: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck the Kobe region on January 17, 1995, killing at least 5,000 people (around 4,600 in Kobe itself) and severely damaging the Port of Kobe, then the world's sixth-largest container port, along with widespread building and infrastructure collapse.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Total damage was estimated at around US$200 billion. The Nikkei 225 plunged 1,025 points the day after the quake, a shock that contributed to speculative trading losses that helped bring down Barings Bank weeks later. Despite the scale of destruction, recovery was rapid: import volumes at the port fully rebounded within a year, and manufacturing activity in greater Kobe reached 98% of its projected pre-quake level by March 1996.

historical_precedents.what_happened: A magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck Christchurch on February 22, 2011, killing 185 people from more than 20 countries and severely damaging the city center, following an earlier, less destructive quake in September 2010.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The combined 2010-2011 Canterbury earthquake sequence caused over NZ$54.8 billion in damage, making it New Zealand's costliest disaster on record and one of the most expensive natural disasters in history relative to the size of the national economy. Christchurch's urban population fell, causing the city to drop from the second- to third-most populous urban area in New Zealand in the years that followed.

historical_precedents.what_happened: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince on January 12, 2010. Death toll estimates vary widely, from roughly 100,000-160,000 in most independent assessments to 220,000-316,000 in the Haitian government's own estimate, reflecting the severe strain the disaster placed on the country's institutions.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Total economic damage was estimated at $7.8-8.5 billion. International emergency fundraising was rapid but limited relative to the scale of destruction: the 'Hope for Haiti Now' telethon raised $58 million within a day, and the American Red Cross mobilized over $2 million in mobile donations in the first 24 hours -- sums that were quickly dwarfed by the reconstruction need in one of the Western Hemisphere's poorest economies.

historical_precedents.what_happened: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck southern Turkey and northern Syria on February 6, 2023, killing between roughly 59,500 and 62,000 people (about 53,500 confirmed in Turkey, 6,000-8,500 in Syria) and leaving an estimated 1.5-2.7 million people homeless.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Damage was estimated at about $150 billion in Turkey (roughly 9% of Turkish GDP) and $9 billion in Syria (roughly 18% of Syria's already war-shrunken GDP), for a combined estimate exceeding $157.8 billion -- illustrating how the same magnitude of earthquake produces very different relative economic damage depending on a country's baseline wealth and construction standards.

possibility_chains: Major earthquakes that destroy ports, factories, or power infrastructure have historically caused sharp but often short-lived shocks to regional manufacturing output and supply chains, since physical rebuilding of critical nodes has in several cases been substantially completed within about a year.

Earthquakes striking economically vulnerable or already-indebted countries have historically produced reconstruction costs large enough, relative to the size of the national economy, to require sustained international aid, concessional financing, or debt relief beyond what domestic fiscal capacity alone could cover.

The same earthquake magnitude has historically produced vastly different death tolls and economic damage depending on a country's building codes and construction quality, meaning the human and financial toll of a quake is only loosely tied to its seismic size.

Financial markets in the affected country have historically reacted with an immediate, sharp sell-off in the day or two after a major earthquake, distinct from the slower-moving real-economy reconstruction effects that follow over subsequent years.

Major earthquakes that destroy ports, factories, or power infrastructure have historically caused sharp but often short-lived shocks to regional manufacturing output and supply chains, since physical rebuilding of critical nodes has in several cases been substantially completed within about a year.

linked_playbooks.name: Natural disaster hitting a manufacturing hub
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Thailand floods (July–November 2011): Global hard-drive prices roughly doubled for several months due to the shortage, and several Japanese automakers had to cut production at plants worldwide because of parts sourced from the flooded factories. A natural disaster affecting a region that supplies a specialized, hard-to-substitute component has historically caused production disruptions for manufacturers worldwide, not just locally, given how concentrated some supply chains are geographically.

linked_playbooks.name: Sovereign government debt default
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's first sovereign default (April 2022): The default followed foreign reserves falling to just $1.9 billion by March 2022, insufficient to cover the country's import and debt-service needs, and led into an IMF rescue program. A sovereign default has historically triggered a sharp loss of access to international capital markets for the defaulting government, often for years, forcing reliance on domestic financing or multilateral lenders in the interim.

linked_playbooks.name: IMF bailout or rescue program for a sovereign
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's IMF Extended Fund Facility after its 2022 default (2022–2024): The program aimed to raise Sri Lanka's tax-to-GDP ratio from 8.1% in 2021 to 15% by 2025, but the accompanying austerity coincided with unemployment rising from 5.7% to 8.3% between 2022 and 2023. IMF rescue programs have historically come attached to austerity conditions (tax increases, spending cuts, structural reforms) that have often produced short-term economic pain — higher unemployment, reduced public services — even where they are intended to restore longer-term stability.

linked_playbooks.name: Major government infrastructure stimulus package
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: European Union's NextGenerationEU recovery fund (2020–2026): Southern European economies received the largest allocations — Greece's share alone approached nearly 20% of its GDP — but implementation also produced documented misuse, including roughly €600 million in fraud schemes uncovered in Italy's allocation in 2024. historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan

ripple_effect.name: Armed conflict driving a large-scale refugee crisis

historical_precedents.what_happened: Syria's civil war displaced millions of people, with neighboring countries absorbing the largest numbers by 2015: Lebanon hosted about 1.1 million registered refugees, Turkey about 800,000 at the time (rising much higher in later years), and Jordan about 600,000. A sharp rise in arrivals to Europe via the Mediterranean and Balkan routes during 2015 became a major political issue across the EU, with Germany emerging as the largest European destination.
historical_precedents.market_impact: A World Bank report found the refugee influx cost Jordan more than $2.5 billion a year, equivalent to about 6% of its GDP, and Jordan's public debt rose to about 95% of GDP by 2016. historical_precedents.market_impact: Ryanair's model was subsequently adopted by other low-cost carriers including easyJet, WestJet, and AirAsia, restructuring competitive pricing across the European aviation market over the following decades.

ripple_effect.name: US territory / sub-sovereign debt restructuring crisis

historical_precedents.event: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring
historical_precedents.what_happened: Puerto Rico's bonds were downgraded to junk status in February 2014, and Governor García Padilla declared the roughly $74 billion in bond debt (plus $49 billion in unfunded pension liabilities) 'not payable' on June 28, 2015; after Puerto Rico missed a $422 million payment on May 1, 2016, Congress passed PROMESA, which President Obama signed June 30, 2016, creating a federal oversight board with authority over the territory's budget and debt restructuring.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022.

possibility_chains: A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

Heavy institutional exposure to a single distressed municipal issuer (in this case, via tax-exempt bond funds that concentrated Puerto Rico debt for its tax advantages) has historically transmitted a regional fiscal crisis into national investment portfolios far from the issuer itself.

Debt-crisis austerity measures layered on top of a shrinking population and tax base have historically been self-reinforcing, since tax increases and service cuts have tended to accelerate the outward migration that shrank the tax base in the first place.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring (2014–2022): Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022. A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

linked_playbooks.name: Major municipal or county bankruptcy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Jefferson County, Alabama bankruptcy (November 2011 – December 2013): The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013. A municipal bankruptcy driven by a shrinking tax base and rising legacy retiree costs has historically forced a choice between deep pension cuts and finding outside funding (such as philanthropic support) to soften them, since the two options are not fiscally separable.

linked_playbooks.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

ripple_effect.name: Electric vehicle transition and automaker manufacturing shift

historical_precedents.what_happened: Tesla's mass-market Model 3, which drew over 325,000 paid reservations within a week of its April 2016 unveiling, entered a severe manufacturing crisis after deliveries began in July 2017; heavy reliance on unproven factory robotics and automation slowed rather than accelerated the assembly line, a period Tesla itself described as 'production hell.'
historical_precedents.market_impact: The prolonged ramp-up strained Tesla's finances and made it one of the most heavily shorted stocks in the market at the time; once resolved by the end of 2018, the Model 3 went on to become the world's best-selling electric car from 2018 to 2021, validating a mass-market EV manufacturing approach that legacy automakers subsequently raced to copy.

historical_precedents.event: General Motors commits to an all-electric future
historical_precedents.what_happened: General Motors announced on January 28, 2021 that it would end production and sales of gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles, including hybrids, by 2035, as part of a broader pledge to reach carbon neutrality by 2040 - one of the most aggressive EV-transition commitments by a legacy automaker at the time.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The announcement accelerated a broader wave of legacy-automaker capital reallocation toward EV production and battery manufacturing; GM and industry peers subsequently scaled back or delayed elements of these targets by the mid-2020s as consumer EV demand growth proved slower than projected, illustrating how quickly manufacturing-investment commitments can reverse when demand assumptions change.

possibility_chains: A large manufacturer's shift toward a new vehicle-propulsion technology has historically required years-long capital investment cycles in new factories and battery supply chains before matching prior production volumes and margins.

Aggressive public EV-transition targets set during periods of strong demand have historically been quietly scaled back once demand growth slows, without necessarily reversing the underlying capital investment already made.

A shift in automaker production toward EVs has historically reduced demand for internal-combustion-engine-specific parts and the workers who make them, even as it creates new demand for battery and software engineering roles.

A large manufacturer's shift toward a new vehicle-propulsion technology has historically required years-long capital investment cycles in new factories and battery supply chains before matching prior production volumes and margins.

linked_playbooks.name: Critical component / chip shortage
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Global automotive semiconductor shortage (2021–2022): Automakers worldwide cut production and, in some cases, shipped vehicles without certain chip-dependent features (like some infotainment options) to be added later; new and used car prices rose noticeably during the shortage. A shortage of a critical, widely-used component has historically forced manufacturers across unrelated industries to cut production simultaneously, since the same component often goes into many different products.

linked_playbooks.name: Critical minerals supply shock for clean energy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's dominance of rare-earth processing and use of export restrictions (2010 onward, escalating through 2025): Rare-earth magnets are a critical input for wind turbine generators and electric-vehicle motors as well as defense systems; the restrictions prompted the US and other countries to accelerate efforts to develop non-Chinese rare-earth mining and processing capacity, and the US moved to bar Chinese-origin rare-earth metals and magnets from defense procurement starting January 2027. A single country's dominance of mining or processing for a specific clean-energy input (nickel, cobalt, lithium, or rare earths) has historically given it outsized leverage over global battery, wind-turbine, or EV-motor supply chains, regardless of where the final products are assembled.

linked_playbooks.name: Import competition and manufacturing employment shock ("China shock")
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: The "China shock" — documented US manufacturing job losses from Chinese import competition (2001 (China's WTO accession) – 2007): The researchers' subsequent 2021 reassessment found the effects concentrated geographically — regions with the heaviest exposure to Chinese import competition saw persistently worse labor-market outcomes for over a decade — while acknowledging that consumers nationally benefited from lower prices, with the researchers estimating only about 6.3% of Americans were net losers once those consumer gains were netted against the concentrated local job losses. Geographically concentrated manufacturing job losses from import competition have historically produced measurable political effects in the affected regions, including documented links between UK regions' exposure to Chinese import competition and their 2016 Brexit vote share, and similar research tying US regional exposure to shifts in presidential voting patterns.

ripple_effect.name: Central bank interest rate cuts

historical_precedents.event: Fed rate cuts during the global financial crisis
historical_precedents.what_happened: As the housing market collapsed and major financial institutions came under stress, the Fed cut its benchmark rate from over 5% to near zero over about 15 months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Despite the cuts, U.S. stocks fell sharply through the crisis (the S&P 500 lost roughly half its value peak-to-trough) as the rate cuts worked to cushion, not prevent, the broader financial and economic damage.

historical_precedents.event: Emergency Fed rate cuts at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Fed cut rates to near zero within weeks as lockdowns froze large parts of the economy.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Along with massive fiscal stimulus, the cuts were followed by a rapid stock market recovery and, over the following two years, a surge in inflation as demand rebounded faster than supply chains could.

historical_precedents.event: Bank of Japan introduces negative interest rates
historical_precedents.what_happened: In a surprise 5–4 vote on January 29, 2016 (effective February 16), the BOJ set a rate of -0.1% on a portion of financial institutions' reserves, reacting to a downgraded inflation outlook driven by falling oil prices — a first for a major central bank outside the Eurozone.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The Nikkei jumped as much as 3% and 10-year JGB yields fell over 9 basis points (later turning negative for the first time) on the announcement, but the yen's initial ~2% slide against the dollar reversed within weeks as safe-haven flows and skepticism about the policy's effectiveness pushed it sharply stronger instead — a reminder that a central bank's intended market reaction doesn't always hold once initial positioning unwinds.

possibility_chains: Lower interest rates have historically made borrowing cheaper, which has often supported home buying, business investment, and stock valuations over time.

Rate cuts made in response to genuine economic distress (as opposed to routine policy adjustment) have historically coincided with continued near-term market weakness, since the cuts are a response to bad conditions, not an immediate fix for them.

Very low rates sustained for an extended period have historically been followed, with a lag, by higher inflation once demand recovers — though the size of that effect has depended heavily on other conditions at the time.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Bank of Japan introduces negative interest rates (January–February 2016): The Nikkei jumped as much as 3% and 10-year JGB yields fell over 9 basis points (later turning negative for the first time) on the announcement, but the yen's initial ~2% slide against the dollar reversed within weeks as safe-haven flows and skepticism about the policy's effectiveness pushed it sharply stronger instead — a reminder that a central bank's intended market reaction doesn't always hold once initial positioning unwinds. Lower interest rates have historically made borrowing cheaper, which has often supported home buying, business investment, and stock valuations over time.

ripple_effect.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships

historical_precedents.what_happened: On 26 July 2023, General Abdourahamane Tchiani led the presidential guard in removing President Mohamed Bazoum and installed a military council. The regional bloc ECOWAS responded with an ultimatum, then sanctions including closed land and air borders, a no-fly zone on commercial flights, suspension of financial transactions, and asset freezes; Nigeria cut electricity supply to Niger on 2 August 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The West African regional central bank cancelled a planned 30 billion CFA franc (about $51 million) bond issuance for Niger, and the World Bank suspended disbursements to the country. Niger is a significant global uranium exporter, and the coup raised questions over the operations of French nuclear fuel company Orano's mining activities there.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected officials. The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military leaders on 11 February 2021 and froze $1 billion in Myanmar government assets held in the U.S.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%.

possibility_chains: A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.
Coups have historically triggered sanctions and suspended aid or financing from regional blocs and international lenders, adding fiscal strain on top of the immediate political disruption.

Foreign companies operating in a country that experiences a coup have historically paused or withdrawn planned investment until the new government's posture toward existing contracts and foreign ownership becomes clearer.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Myanmar military coup (February 2021): Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%. A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

linked_playbooks.name: Diplomatic rupture between major regional powers
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia severs relations with Iran (January 2016): The rupture deepened the broader Saudi-Iran regional rivalry playing out through proxy conflicts in Yemen, Syria, and elsewhere; relations were not restored until a China-brokered agreement announced 10 March 2023, with embassies reopening in Riyadh in June 2023 and Tehran in August 2023. A sudden severing of diplomatic relations between neighboring major economies has historically disrupted direct trade, aviation, and financial flows between them, forcing rerouting of commerce through third countries at added cost.

linked_playbooks.name: Sharp currency devaluation / currency crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Turkish lira crisis (2018): The lira lost roughly 30–40% of its value against the U.S. dollar over the year, sharply raising the cost of imports and foreign-currency debt for Turkish businesses. A sharp currency devaluation has historically made imported goods, including fuel and food, significantly more expensive for consumers and businesses in the affected country.
